summary:
South Sudan's Penal Code reaches gender presentation directly. Section 379 criminalises "any male person who dresses or is attired in the fashion of a woman" and carries up to three months' imprisonment. The provision turns on appearance alone: it requires no sexual conduct and no disclosure of identity, so a trans visitor presenting female is exposed in public rather than only in private.

The same code treats consensual same-sex sexual conduct as an "unnatural offense", defined as carnal intercourse against the order of nature, punishable by up to 10 years' imprisonment. Where the conduct is nonconsensual the maximum rises to 14 years.

United States State Department country reports for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2022 each record that no authorities were reported to have enforced the same-sex conduct provision. Those reports describe no repeal, no moratorium and no prosecutorial policy limiting its use, so the exposure is statutory rather than evidenced in prosecutions. The most recent report held in this record is the 2022 edition; no later reporting is available here.

The same 2018 to 2022 reporting period records security forces harassing LGBTQI+ people and at times arresting, detaining, torturing and beating them. Abuse by state agents is documented alongside the unenforced statute, so the absence of prosecutions under the Penal Code does not describe how security personnel treat a visible visitor.

Staff of Access for All, an LGBTQ-supportive organisation, were detained for several months after a security force raid in 2017 and released without charge. The organisation was intimidated into closing that year and its executive director left the country.

In September 2017 the minister for Labour, Public Service and Human Resource Development, Gathoth Gatkuoth Hothnyang, said the government would order security forces to arrest LGBTQ people and detain them until they procreate. No such arrests were reported by the end of that year.

The State Department's 2022 report found that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled South Sudan because of actively hostile government rhetoric and action. An earlier official statement in the same vein is then-President Salva Kiir Mayardit's July 2010 remark that homosexuality is not in the "character" of Southern Sudanese people and would never gain support.

South Sudan has no hate-crime or anti-discrimination legislation protecting LGBTQ people from harassment or abuse on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity. The single exception noted is that, as of 2020, harassment of employees on those grounds is prohibited for oil and gas companies operating in the country.

Same-sex couples have no legal recognition, and same-sex marriage has been barred by the Constitution since 2011. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read locally as same-sex therefore has no route to recognition of a partner.

No LGBTQ-support organisation is known to be operating in the country. The Non-Governmental Organisations Act (2016) bars organisations from contravening the country's sovereignty, institutions and laws, which constrains LGBTQ-supportive civic groups given that same-sex activity is illegal.
tangentialFactors:
Societal hostility is recorded separately from state action. The 2011 State Department report found "widespread" societal discrimination against gay men and lesbians; that figure is a historical snapshot and no later prevalence measure appears in this inventory.

Hostility has been voiced from religious and political leadership as well. In 2006 bishop Abraham Mayom Athiaan split from the Episcopal Church of Sudan over what he judged insufficient condemnation of homosexuality, and the 2010 presidential statement placed the question outside national "character".

The inventory contains no trans-specific violence count, killing rate or survey of trans people, so no comparison against South Sudan's general homicide rate can be made here. Enforcement non-reporting in the State Department series is an absence of reported prosecutions, not a finding of safety, and it sits beside documented security-force detention and beating over the same 2018 to 2022 window.
localsOnly:
Residents live under the same Section 379 appearance offence and the same 10-year and 14-year "unnatural offense" ceilings that apply to visitors, with the added exposure of being identifiable within a small population.

Organised support has been dismantled rather than merely absent. Access for All was raided in 2017, its staff held for months without charge, and the group closed under intimidation; its executive director left the country. The 2016 NGOs Act gives the authorities a general ground to act against groups deemed to contravene the country's sovereignty, institutions and laws.

Employment protection is narrow. As of 2020 the only documented prohibition on harassment by sexual orientation or gender identity applies to oil and gas companies operating in the country; no wider labour or anti-discrimination statute is recorded.

The 2022 State Department finding that most openly LGBTQI+ citizens had fled describes a resident population that has already been displaced by official rhetoric and action, which shapes what community and informal support remains inside the country.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: this inventory holds nothing on gender marker or passport rules, entry and visa screening, customs or airport treatment of gender-nonconforming travellers, access to hormone therapy or trans-related healthcare, or legal status of gender-affirming care. None of these can be stated either way from the sources held.

Unresolved: no court decisions, charging records or case law interpreting Section 379 or the "unnatural offense" provisions appear here, so how the dress offence has been applied in practice is not sourced. The five State Department reports establish only that enforcement was not reported to them.

Unresolved: the most recent documentation in this record closes with the 2022 State Department report. Whether the security-force conduct described for 2018 to 2022, the 2017 detention threat, or the 2017 closure of Access for All has continued or changed after 2022 is not sourced, and no later reporting is available to confirm or deny it.

Unresolved: no trans-specific violence statistics, denominators or per-capita comparisons are held for South Sudan, so no magnitude of trans-specific risk can be stated.
